title: Cancer epitope prediction tools and analysis pipelines in CEDAR.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded CEDAR's T cell assay export (14.4 MB zip, one 360 MB file tcell_full_v3.csv, zip entry dated 2026-09-24) and streamed all of it: 156,403 assay rows, 162 columns with a two-row header, 67,672 distinct epitope names, 4,021 distinct PubMed IDs. Label column 'Assay|Qualitative Measurement' = 87,899 Negative / 59,516 Positive / 6,255 Positive-Low / 1,976 Positive-High / 757 Positive-Intermediate. 30,601 rows carry a mutation annotation (neoepitopes). Restricting to human host, MHC class I, 8-11mer peptides with a 4-digit HLA-A/B/C allele and a non-prediction evidence code gives 24,095 rows -> 8,029 unique (peptide, allele) pairs, of which 1,568 (19.5%) carry both a Positive and a Negative call. 103 alleles, only 10 with >=200 rows, HLA-A*02:01 = 12,811 of 24,095 rows. Publication year present, 45 distinct years through 2026. Also queried the IEDB query API (https://query-api.iedb.org/tcell_search) and read a count header: 578,238 T cell assay rows in the parent IEDB. Licence CC-BY 4.0 read from the JSON-LD block on the CEDAR export page.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The description of the nextgen-tools pipelines and which predictors they wrap (NetMHCpan, NetMHCIIpan, MHCflurry, PRIME, ICERFIRE, IMPROVE, TCRMatch). Europe PMC's supplementary-file endpoint timed out, so the supplement was not retrievable. Published benchmark AUC values for competing tools came from retrieved search results, not from files I opened.

a1_downloadable.note: No login: the export zip downloaded straight from cedar.iedb.org and opened. Export page carries a CC-BY 4.0 licence tag.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Checked in the file: 'Assay|Qualitative Measurement' holds Positive/Positive-Low/-Intermediate/-High/Negative on every one of the 156,403 rows. Only choice needed is how to binarise.

a3_inputs_present.note: Peptide amino acid sequence is in 'Epitope|Name' and the HLA allele in 'MHC Restriction|Name' - no accession lookups needed for the core task.

a4_units_stated.note: Primary label is a documented category, not a number. The numeric column is only filled on 2,732 of 156,403 rows and mixes nM, 1/s, M^-1s^-1 and angstroms, so it is unusable as a label.

a5_enough_rows.note: 156,403 assay rows counted; the clean class I human 8-11mer subset is 8,029 unique peptide-allele pairs (6,461 after dropping contradictory ones).

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 14.4 MB zip; 360 MB CSV streamed; ~0.4 GB in memory for the subset
a6_fits_laptop.note: Streamed the whole CSV with Python's csv module in under a minute; no GPU needed for peptides of 8-11 residues.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The paper is a tools description and states no row counts, so there is nothing to contradict. CEDAR export (156,403) is properly smaller than the parent IEDB count from the API (578,238).

a8_label_provenance.note: Label is a real T cell assay outcome (ELISPOT 58,731, multimer/tetramer 23,409, ICS 14,295 and others). Caveat verified in the file: the HLA restriction - a feature - is itself a prediction on 17,535 rows ('MHC binding prediction' evidence code), so that subset must be dropped.

B1.why: One CSV inside the zip, though 162 columns wide; verified in the file.

B2.why: Two-row header and 360 MB size force streaming; otherwise parsed first try.

B3.why: Positive/Negative comparable after binarising, but spans 15 assay methods; no author normalisation.

B4.why: Positive-Low/-Intermediate/-High (8,988 rows) need a policy; numeric column mostly empty.

B5.why: 1,568 of 8,029 clean peptide-allele pairs (19.5%) hold contradictory Positive and Negative calls.

B6.why: Column names self-describing, but evidence codes are ontology IRIs and 162 columns are undocumented in-file.

C1.why: Transfer-decay framing is informative, but the obvious project is beating a published AUC.

C2.why: BigMHC, PRIME, DeepImmuno, IMPROVE, ICERFIRE all open and already benchmarked on CEDAR itself.

C3.why: Found a public repo already pairing ESM-2 embeddings with curated IEDB/CEDAR immunogenicity data.

C4.why: T cell assays are costly, but prediction is already cheap and served by many free tools.

C5.why: Published CEDAR-benchmark AUCs retrieved: IEDB 0.555, IMPROVE 0.624, ICERFIRE 0.726.

D1.why: ESM-2, an open-weight protein language model, directly fits short peptide sequences.

D2.why: 8-11 residue peptides; ~8k embeddings cacheable once on a laptop CPU in minutes.

D3.why: ESM-2 weights are MIT; CEDAR export page declares CC-BY 4.0 (read in its JSON-LD).

E1.why: Can hold out by source protein, allele or publication ID - all present as columns.

E2.why: 1,225 distinct publications and 103 alleles in the class I subset; 10 alleles have >=200 rows.

E3.why: Majority-class dummy computable: 3,912 positive vs 2,549 negative clean pairs.

E4.why: The 1,568 contradictory peptide-allele pairs give a direct measured noise floor.

E5.why: HLA-A*02:01 anchor preference and known MART-1 epitope ELAGIGILTV (seen in file) must be recovered.

E6.why: Label shuffling and allele-only/peptide-only ablations are trivial on a single table.

E7.why: Reference year column spans 45 years to 2026 (7,744 rows from 2025), so temporal split is one line.

E8.why: IMPROVE's published CEDAR benchmark (2,436 peptides, RankEL<2) could be reconstructed; not attempted.

G1.why: 106,735 rows carry a UniProt-style parent-protein IRI plus NCBI taxonomy and allele ontology IRIs.

G2.why: UniProt/AlphaFold DB on the parent protein and GTEx/Human Protein Atlas on gene expression are joinable.

G3.why: Peptide to parent protein is clean one-to-many, but 49,668 rows have no parent IRI at all.

G4.why: Does tumour-antigen expression add to sequence? Partly answered already by IMPROVE's feature set.

H1.why: 87,899 Negative rows counted - failures are systematically curated, not just hits.

H2.why: 4,021 publications (diverse labs) but HLA-A*02:01 is 53% of class I rows and host is 81% human.

H3.why: Honest claim statable in one sentence; the selection bias is visible in the evidence-code column.

H4.why: Evidence codes expose predicted-allele rows, but this tools paper never discusses dataset gaps.

I1.why: Named groups: Gfeller lab (PRIME), Nielsen lab (ICERFIRE), Karchin lab (BigMHC), CEDAR team itself.

I2.why: Would only change peptide shortlisting if it clearly beat BigMHC/PRIME, which is unlikely.

I3.why: Users need precision in a top-20 shortlist; AUC on 6,461 pairs is only roughly that.

I4.why: Machine learning helps, but a binding-predictor rank threshold already captures much of the signal.

J1.why: Real grouped splits, temporal validation, frozen-backbone embeddings - the ML I want to practise.

J2.why: HLA anchor motifs give a sanity check, but immunogenicity intuition needs an immunologist.

J3.why: A cleaned CEDAR table with its 19.5% label-conflict statistic is shareable even if the model fails.

J4.why: No time budget stated anywhere for this candidate.

J5.why: No kill date or condition written down.

existing_models.name: BigMHC (deep learning predictor of peptide-MHC presentation and immunogenicity)
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved description reports higher precision than seven other models on immunogenic neoepitopes after transfer learning; exact split not read from the paper itself.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Immunogenicity data scarcity relative to presentation data; they use transfer learning precisely because immunogenicity labels are few.

existing_models.name: PRIME (predictor of immunogenic class I epitopes, Gfeller lab)
existing_models.score_and_split: No number retrieved; code on GitHub, free for academic non-commercial use.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Separating T cell receptor recognition propensity from MHC binding.

existing_models.name: DeepImmuno (deep learning immunogenicity predictor)
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved review ranks it top by false-detection rate on one validation set and worst on the ITSNdb set - i.e. unstable across datasets.

existing_models.name: IMPROVE (feature model for neoepitope immunogenicity)
existing_models.score_and_split: AUC 0.624 on a CEDAR-derived independent benchmark of 2,436 peptides (548 immunogenic), filtered to predicted binding rank <2; best tool on that set per the retrieved paper.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Weak absolute performance - AUC near 0.62 means most shortlisted peptides are still wrong.

existing_models.name: ICERFIRE (neoepitope immunogenicity predictor)
existing_models.score_and_split: AUC 0.726 on independent neoepitope datasets per retrieved search result; split details not read in the source paper.

existing_models.name: NetMHCpan-4.1 / NetMHCIIpan / MHCflurry (binding and presentation predictors wrapped by the CEDAR pipelines)
existing_models.score_and_split: The paper under evaluation reports IEDB's own immunogenicity tool at AUC 0.555 on CEDAR-style data per the retrieved benchmark; these tools define the baseline shortlisting step.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Going beyond binding to actual T cell recognition - stated as the central challenge in this paper's own abstract.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model; esm2_t12_35M or t33_650M checkpoint)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU: ~8k peptides of 8-11 residues embed in minutes

integration.partner_dataset: UniProt / AlphaFold DB on the parent protein, plus GTEx or Human Protein Atlas tissue expression for the source gene
integration.join_key: UniProt accession parsed from 'Epitope|Molecule Parent IRI' (present on 106,735 of 156,403 rows)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does how much, and where, the parent protein is expressed explain which tumour peptides actually trigger T cells, over and above the peptide sequence itself?

controls.positive_control: Model must recover the HLA-A*02:01 anchor preference (hydrophobic residue at position 2 and position 9) and call the known MART-1 melanoma epitope ELAGIGILTV - present in the file - immunogenic.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle labels within each allele and confirm collapse to the per-allele majority rate; ablate to allele-only and peptide-only feature blocks.
controls.external_validation: Temporal split on the reference-year column (train pre-2020, test the 7,744 rows from 2025 and 1,564 from 2026), plus the parent IEDB's 578,238 non-cancer T cell assays as a second source.

honest_claim_h3: Among peptides that somebody chose to test - 53% of them HLA-A*02:01, most shortlisted by a binding predictor first - the peptide sequence plus allele predicts whether a published T cell assay was scored positive, with a ceiling set by the 19.5% of peptide-allele pairs on which labs disagree.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a short peptide's amino acid sequence and the patient's immune-presentation molecule type to predict whether human T cells responded to it.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per published immune assay: the peptide sequence (8-11 amino acids), its HLA (human leukocyte antigen) type, and the source protein. 156,403 rows total; 8,029 unique peptide-allele pairs survive filtering to human class I assays with an experimentally determined allele, 6,461 after dropping pairs where labs disagree.
plain_idea.predict: A yes/no immunogenicity call. The truth comes from laboratory T cell assays curated from 4,021 publications - mostly ELISPOT (58,731 rows), tetramer staining (23,409) and intracellular cytokine staining (14,295) - recorded in the column 'Assay|Qualitative Measurement'.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Cancer vaccine and cell-therapy groups must pick ~20 peptides per patient from thousands of candidates, and today's tools reach only about 0.62-0.73 area-under-curve on this very data. Even a failed attempt would quantify how much of the remaining error is irreducible disagreement between labs.

label_elsewhere.sources: IEDB, the parent database of CEDAR - I queried its API and read a count of 578,238 T cell assay rows. Also VDJdb, McPAS-TCR and ITSNdb (known resources holding T cell recognition data; named in retrieved benchmark papers, not opened by me).
label_elsewhere.join_key: Peptide amino acid sequence plus HLA allele name (standard IMGT/MRO nomenclature, e.g. HLA-A*02:01)
label_elsewhere.why: The same assay outcome is recorded for hundreds of thousands of non-cancer peptides, so a cancer-trained model can be tested on infectious-disease epitopes and vice versa - but it also means every existing tool already has this training data.

ml_idea: Freeze ESM-2 (protein language model), embed the 8-11mer peptide, concatenate a learned HLA allele representation, and train a small classifier on the 6,461 non-contradictory human class I peptide-allele pairs from CEDAR; evaluate with a source-protein grouped split and a temporal split on publication year, against BigMHC and PRIME as runnable baselines and the published CEDAR-benchmark AUCs (IEDB 0.555, IMPROVE 0.624, ICERFIRE 0.726). The one genuinely non-losable sub-result is measuring the label noise floor directly from the 1,568 contradictory pairs and reporting how much of the field's reported error that explains.

effort.compute_note: Timed the actual streaming parse of the 360 MB CSV (under a minute, trivial RAM). Embedding and cross-validation times are estimates for ~8k peptides of 8-11 residues with a small ESM-2 checkpoint on a laptop CPU; not timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the unique (peptide, HLA allele) pairs in the human class I 8-11mer subset and how many carry contradictory calls. Done: 8,029 pairs, 1,568 (19.5%) contradictory, leaving 6,461 - smaller than what BigMHC and PRIME already train on.

verdict_reason: Part A passes cleanly and the data is genuinely open (CC-BY 4.0, 156,403 curated assay rows with 87,899 negatives, a year column and UniProt links), but the project dies on Part C and Part B. C2 is as saturated as it gets: BigMHC, PRIME, DeepImmuno, IMPROVE and ICERFIRE are open, published, and have already been benchmarked on CEDAR itself (AUC 0.555-0.726), and I found a public repository already combining ESM-2 embeddings with curated IEDB/CEDAR immunogenicity labels, so the planned angle is taken. Model-readiness is worse than it looks: the usable class I subset is only 8,029 unique peptide-allele pairs and 19.5% of them carry contradictory Positive and Negative calls across labs, which caps achievable performance near where the published tools already sit. The paper itself is a software description with no new dataset and no retrievable supplement, so there is no fresh measurement to exploit.
